title: Conditional Probability, Independence and Bayes’ Rule

intro.x: Probabilities change when we learn something. The probability that a card is the ace of spades is $1/52$; once we are told that it is black, it is $1/26$. This chapter makes that idea precise, and develops the three tools that follow from it: the multiplication rule, the law of total probability, and Bayes’ rule. We then define independence, the situation where learning one fact tells us nothing about another.

blocks.x: Suppose $\Omega$ is finite with equally likely outcomes, and we are told that the event $B$ has occurred. The outcome is now equally likely to be any element of $B$, and the event $A$ occurs exactly when the outcome lies in $A\cap B$. So the natural updated probability is

\frac{\abs{A\cap B}}{\abs{B}}=\frac{\abs{A\cap B}/\abs\Omega}{\abs B/\abs\Omega}
=\frac{\Prob(A\cap B)}{\Prob(B)}.
The right-hand side makes sense on any probability space, which motivates the following definition.
Let $B$ be an event with $\Prob(B)>0$. The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is
\Prob(A\given B)=\frac{\Prob(A\cap B)}{\Prob(B)}.

If $\Prob(B)>0$, the function $A\mapsto\Prob(A\given B)$ is a probability measure on $(\Omega,\F)$. Consequently every result of Chapter 2 holds with $\Prob(\cdot)$ replaced by $\Prob(\cdot\given B)$.

Non-negativity is clear. Normalisation: $\Prob(\Omega\given B)=\Prob(B)/\Prob(B)=1$. For countable additivity, let $A_1,A_2,\dots$ be pairwise disjoint. The events $A_i\cap B$ are also pairwise disjoint, with $\bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\bigr)\cap B=\bigcup_i(A_i\cap B)$, so

\Prob\Bigl(\bigcup_iA_i\given B\Bigr)
=\frac{\sum_i\Prob(A_i\cap B)}{\Prob(B)}=\sum_i\Prob(A_i\given B).

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: conditioning on events of probability zero

blocks.x: The definition requires $\Prob(B)>0$. Conditioning on an event of probability zero is not simply “undefined”: for continuous random variables one conditions on $\{X=x\}$, which has probability zero, and obtains perfectly meaningful answers. This requires a different construction (conditional densities in Chapter 8 and conditional expectation in Chapter 10, made fully rigorous in Chapter 15). Until then, all conditioning events have positive probability.

In general $\Prob(A\given B)\ne\Prob(B\given A)$. The two quantities share the numerator $\Prob(A\cap B)$ but have different denominators. For example, almost every Olympic sprinter is a good runner, but few good runners are Olympic sprinters. Confusing the two is the single most common error in applied probability; the examples at the end of Section 3.3 show its consequences.

sections.title: The multiplication rule and total probability

blocks.x: Rearranging the definition gives a rule for the probability of a joint event.
If $\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1})>0$, then

\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n)
=\Prob(A_1)\,\Prob(A_2\given A_1)\,\Prob(A_3\given A_1\cap A_2)\cdots
\Prob(A_n\given A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1}).
Write each conditional probability as a ratio. The product telescopes:

\Prob(A_1)\cdot\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2)}{\Prob(A_1)}\cdot
\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)}{\Prob(A_1\cap A_2)}\cdots
\frac{\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n)}{\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1})}
=\Prob(A_1\cap\dots\cap A_n).

All denominators are positive: for each $k\le n-1$ we have $A_1\cap\dots\cap A_k\supseteq A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1}$, so by monotonicity (Proposition 2.4(iv)) its probability is at least that of $A_1\cap\dots\cap A_{n-1}$, which is positive by hypothesis.
An urn has $5$ red and $3$ blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Let $R_i$ be “the $i$th ball is red”. Then
\Prob(R_1\cap R_2)=\Prob(R_1)\Prob(R_2\given R_1)=\frac58\cdot\frac47=\frac5{14}.
Let $B_1,B_2,\dots$ be a finite or countable partition of $\Omega$ with $\Prob(B_i)>0$ for every $i$. Then for every event $A$,
\Prob(A)=\sum_i\Prob(A\given B_i)\,\Prob(B_i).

The events $A\cap B_i$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is $A$ (because the $B_i$ cover $\Omega$). By countable additivity, $\Prob(A)=\sum_i\Prob(A\cap B_i)$, and by the definition of conditional probability $\Prob(A\cap B_i)=\Prob(A\given B_i)\Prob(B_i)$.

The law of total probability embodies a strategy: split a hard problem into cases according to a partition, solve each case, and average with weights $\Prob(B_i)$. It is the starting point for first-step analysis, which we use extensively for random walks and Markov chains.
Urn I has $2$ red and $3$ blue balls; urn II has $4$ red and $1$ blue. An urn is chosen with equal probability, then a ball is drawn at random from it. With $B_1,B_2$ the events “urn I”, “urn II”,
\Prob(\text{red})=\frac25\cdot\frac12+\frac45\cdot\frac12=\frac35 .
Let $B_1,B_2,\dots$ be a partition of $\Omega$ with $\Prob(B_i)>0$, and let $A$ be an event with $\Prob(A)>0$. Then for each $j$,
\Prob(B_j\given A)=\frac{\Prob(A\given B_j)\Prob(B_j)}{\sum_i\Prob(A\given B_i)\Prob(B_i)} .
By definition, $\Prob(B_j\given A)=\Prob(A\cap B_j)/\Prob(A)$ and $\Prob(A\cap B_j)=\Prob(A\given B_j)\Prob(B_j)$. Replace $\Prob(A)$ in the denominator using Theorem 3.5.

In words: the posterior probability of a hypothesis $B_j$ after seeing the evidence $A$ is proportional to the prior $\Prob(B_j)$ times the likelihood $\Prob(A\given B_j)$, and the denominator simply normalises. For two hypotheses it is convenient to use odds.
For events $B$ and $A$ with $0<\Prob(B)<1$ and $\Prob(A)>0$,

\frac{\Prob(B\given A)}{\Prob(B^c\given A)}
=\frac{\Prob(B)}{\Prob(B^c)}\cdot\frac{\Prob(A\given B)}{\Prob(A\given B^c)} .
That is, posterior odds $=$ prior odds $\times$ likelihood ratio.
Apply the ratio form of Bayes’ rule to $B$ and $B^c$; the common denominator $\Prob(A)$ cancels.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: A medical test and the base rate

blocks.x: A disease affects $1\%$ of a population. A test returns positive for $99\%$ of people with the disease (sensitivity) and for $5\%$ of people without it (false positive rate). A random person tests positive. What is the probability they have the disease? Let $D$ be “has the disease” and $+$ “tests positive”. Then

Even though the test is accurate, only about one positive in six is a true case, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones. In odds form: the prior odds are $1:99$ and the likelihood ratio is $0.99/0.05=19.8$, so the posterior odds are $19.8:99=1:5$, which is $1/6$ again.

Many people answer “about $95$–$99\%$” in Example 3.9, treating $\Prob(+\given D)$ as if it were $\Prob(D\given +)$. The correct answer needs the prior $\Prob(D)$. A useful sanity check: imagine $10{,}000$ people. About $100$ have the disease and $99$ of them test positive; of the $9{,}900$ healthy, about $495$ test positive. Among about $594$ positives, $99$ are sick.

Suppose a DNA profile matches a randomly chosen innocent person with probability $10^{-6}$, and a crime is committed in a city of $10^7$ people, one of whom is the culprit and matches with certainty. A suspect is found only because the profile matched. The probability of the evidence if the suspect is innocent is $10^{-6}$, but that is not the probability of innocence. Among the roughly $10^7\cdot10^{-6}=10$ innocent people who would also match, plus the guilty one, only about $1$ in $11$ matches is the culprit, if no other evidence distinguishes them. Treating $\Prob(\text{evidence}\given\text{innocent})$ as $\Prob(\text{innocent}\given\text{evidence})$ is exactly the confusion in the pitfall above.

Behind one of three doors is a car; behind the others, goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other two doors, always revealing a goat, and if both remaining doors hide goats he picks one at random. Should you switch?

Let $C_i$ be “car behind door $i$”, each with probability $1/3$, and let $H$ be the event that the host opens door 3. Then $\Prob(H\given C_1)=1/2$, $\Prob(H\given C_2)=1$ (he must avoid the car), and $\Prob(H\given C_3)=0$. By total probability $\Prob(H)=\frac13(\frac12+1+0) =\frac12$, and by Bayes’ rule

\Prob(C_1\given H)=\frac{\frac12\cdot\frac13}{\frac12}=\frac13,\qquad
\Prob(C_2\given H)=\frac{1\cdot\frac13}{\frac12}=\frac23 .
Switching to door 2 wins with probability $2/3$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the answer depends on the host’s protocol

blocks.x: Monty Hall is famous because its answer depends on a sentence that is easy to skip: the host knows where the car is and always reveals a goat. Suppose instead that the host opens one of the two unchosen doors at random, and we observe that he happened to reveal a goat. Then $\Prob(\text{goat shown}\given C_1)=1$ but $\Prob(\text{goat shown}\given C_2)=\Prob(\text{goat shown}\given C_3)=1/2$, so the probability that your original door wins, given that a goat was shown, is
\frac{\frac13\cdot1}{\frac13\cdot1+\frac23\cdot\frac12}=\frac12,

and switching gives no advantage. The same observed event (“door 3 shows a goat”) has different probabilities under different protocols. In general, to condition correctly you must model how the information arrived, not just the information.

“A family has two children. At least one is a boy. What is the probability both are boys?” With $\Omega=\{BB,BG,GB,GG\}$ equally likely, conditioning on “at least one boy” leaves $\{BB,BG,GB\}$, so the answer is $1/3$. If instead we are told that the older child is a boy, only $\{BB,BG\}$ remain and the answer is $1/2$. If we are told only that we met one of the children and it was a boy, the answer depends on how that child was chosen. As with Monty Hall, the wording specifies the information-gathering process, and different processes give different answers.

Informally, $A$ and $B$ are independent if learning that $B$ occurred does not change the probability of $A$: $\Prob(A\given B)=\Prob(A)$. Writing this as $\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B)$ removes the need for $\Prob(B)>0$ and makes the definition symmetric.
Events $A$ and $B$ are independent if $\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)\Prob(B)$.
If $A$ and $B$ are independent, then so are $A$ and $B^c$, $A^c$ and $B$, and $A^c$ and $B^c$.
$\Prob(A\cap B^c)=\Prob(A)-\Prob(A\cap B)=\Prob(A)-\Prob(A)\Prob(B) =\Prob(A)\Prob(B^c)$. The other two follow by applying this result again.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: independent is not the same as disjoint

blocks.x: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and both have positive probability, they are dependent: $\Prob(A\cap B)=0\ne\Prob(A)\Prob(B)$. Indeed, learning that $B$ occurred tells you that $A$ did not. Independence is about information, not about set overlap.
For more than two events, the right definition requires every sub-collection to factor.
Events $A_1,\dots,A_n$ are mutually independent if for every sub-collection of indices $i_1<\dots
\Prob(A_{i_1}\cap\dots\cap A_{i_k})=\Prob(A_{i_1})\cdots\Prob(A_{i_k}).
This is $2^n-n-1$ conditions. An infinite family is mutually independent if every finite sub-family is.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Pairwise independent but not mutually independent

blocks.x: Toss two fair coins. Let $A$ = “first is heads”, $B$ = “second is heads”, $C$ = “both tosses agree”. Then $\Prob(A)=\Prob(B)=\Prob(C)=1/2$. Each pairwise intersection is $\{HH\}$ with probability $1/4=\frac12\cdot\frac12$, so the events are pairwise independent. But $A\cap B\cap C=\{HH\}$ has probability $1/4$, not $1/8$. Knowing any two of the events determines the third.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: checking only pairs is not enough

blocks.x: Pairwise independence is strictly weaker than mutual independence. Many results (laws of large numbers, concentration inequalities) hold under pairwise independence, but others (such as the product formula for the probability that none of the events occurs) require mutual independence. Always state which one you are using.

Independent trials each succeeding with probability $p$ model repeated experiments such as coin tosses. The probability of exactly $k$ successes in $n$ trials is obtained by noting that each particular sequence with $k$ successes has probability $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$ (by mutual independence), and there are $\binom nk$ such sequences (Theorem 1.12):
\Prob(k\text{ successes})=\binom nk p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.
This is the binomial distribution, studied in Chapter 5.
Given an event $C$ with $\Prob(C)>0$, events $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ if $\Prob(A\cap B\given C)=\Prob(A\given C)\Prob(B\given C)$.
This is independence under the probability measure $\Prob(\cdot\given C)$, which Theorem 3.2 shows is a legitimate measure.

Two coins: coin 1 shows heads with probability $0.9$, coin 2 with probability $0.1$. Choose a coin with equal probability, then toss it twice. Given the coin, the tosses are independent. Unconditionally, let $H_1,H_2$ be “heads on toss 1/2”. Then $\Prob(H_1)=\Prob(H_2)=\frac12(0.9+0.1)=0.5$ but
The first toss is informative about which coin we hold, and therefore about the second toss.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: independence and conditional independence are logically unrelated

blocks.x: Conditional independence given $C$ does not imply independence (previous example), and independence does not imply conditional independence. For instance, two independent fair coin tosses become dependent when conditioned on the event “at least one head”. Learning that a third variable is related to both can create or destroy dependence. This phenomenon underlies Simpson’s paradox below, and appears in Bayesian networks and causal inference.
A well-known data set (Charig et al., 1986) compares two kidney-stone treatments by success counts:

Treatment A is better within each stone size, yet B has the higher overall rate. Law of total probability explains it: the overall success rate is $\Prob(S\given T)=\sum_z\Prob(S\given T,Z=z)\Prob(Z=z\given T)$, a weighted average of the group rates, and the weights $\Prob(Z=z\given T)$ differ: A was used mostly on large (harder) stones, B mostly on small ones. No arithmetic is wrong; the aggregate comparison simply mixes the effect of the treatment with the effect of case difficulty.

Two cards are dealt from a standard deck. Find the probability that the second card is an ace given that the first is an ace, and then the probability that the second is an ace given that the first is not an ace. Use total probability to show that the unconditional probability that the second card is an ace is $1/13$.
Prove that if $\Prob(A\given B)>\Prob(A)$ then $\Prob(B\given A)>\Prob(B)$ (assuming positive probabilities), and that $\Prob(A\given B^c)<\Prob(A)$.

A test for a condition has sensitivity $95\%$ and false positive rate $2\%$. In which populations (prevalence) does a positive result give at least a $50\%$ probability of the condition? Solve using odds.
Prove that $A$ is independent of itself if and only if $\Prob(A)\in\{0,1\}$.
Prove that if $A$ and $B$ are independent and $A$ and $C$ are independent, it need not follow that $A$ and $B\cap C$ are independent. (Use Example 3.15.)
Show that if $A_1,\dots,A_n$ are mutually independent then $\Prob(\bigcup A_i)=1-\prod(1-\Prob(A_i))$.

(Gambler’s ruin warm-up) You start with $1$ unit and bet $1$ unit on fair coin tosses until you have $0$ or $3$ units. Let $h_k$ be the probability of reaching $3$ from $k$. Use the law of total probability on the first toss to write equations for $h_1,h_2$ and solve them.

Three prisoners problem: one of three prisoners $A,B,C$ will be pardoned at random. $A$ asks the guard to name one of the other two who will not be pardoned. The guard names $B$. Under the assumption that if both $B$ and $C$ are not pardoned the guard picks one at random, what is the probability that $A$ is pardoned? Compare with the case where the guard always names $B$ when possible.

(Challenge) Let $A_1,A_2,\dots$ be mutually independent with $\Prob(A_i)=p_i$. Show that $\Prob(\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty A_i^c)=\prod_{i=1}^\infty(1-p_i)$ using continuity of probability, and show that this product is positive if and only if $\sum p_i<\infty$ (assuming all $p_i<1$).
